blogs.title: The Objective Observer in the Age of Satire: *Santos v. Kimmel* and the Irrelevance of Subjective Intent Post-*Warhol*
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Second Circuit's rigorous application of the 'transformative use' test, specifically focusing on how the court disentangled the creator's subjective intent from the objective perception of the work. By rejecting Santos's argument that Kimmel 'designed' the original purpose of the videos by instigating their creation, the opinion reinforces the Supreme Court's holding in *Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith*: fair use turns on what a reasonable observer perceives, not the artist's or provocateur's internal motivation. The piece will explore how this objective standard provides robust protection for satirists who engage subjects to create self-incriminating or absurd content, ensuring that the 'trap' set by a comedian does not negate the transformative nature of the resulting commentary.

blogs.title: Bad Faith No More? The Erosion of the 'Good Faith' Requirement in Fair Use Doctrine
blogs.description: Focusing on a pivotal doctrinal shift, this article examines the court's explicit rejection of Santos's argument that Kimmel's deceptive tactics (using fictitious names) constituted 'bad faith' that should nullify the fair use defense. While *Harper & Row* famously stated that fair use presupposes good faith, the Second Circuit notes the Supreme Court has since distanced itself from this rigid requirement. The post will discuss the implications of decoupling ethical conduct during acquisition from the legal analysis of transformation, signaling a trend where courts prioritize the expressive value of the secondary work over the morality of the methods used to obtain the source material, provided there is no intent to supplant the market.

blogs.title: The Platform Paradox: Why Third-Party Beneficiary Claims Fail in Digital Marketplace Disputes
blogs.description: Moving beyond copyright, this post dissects the dismissal of Santos's state law contract claims to highlight a critical gap in digital liability. The court held that Santos, as a content creator on Cameo, could not enforce the platform's Terms of Service against a user (Kimmel) because he was not a party to that contract and lacked third-party beneficiary status. The analysis will delve into the strict privity requirements under Illinois and New York law applied here, illustrating how current contractual frameworks often leave individual creators without recourse when platforms fail to police user behavior, effectively insulating bad actors who exploit technical loopholes in Terms of Service agreements.
